NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__Neurophysiology:
Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) together form neurophysiology's core toolkit for characterising peripheral nerve and muscle disease. NCS stimulate a nerve and record the evoked response to quantify conduction velocity, amplitude and latency; needle EMG samples electrical activity within muscle at rest and on contraction. Their central job is to separate an axonal process (nerve fibres are lost) from a demyelinating one (the myelin sheath is damaged but axons persist), and to localise the lesion to root, plexus, nerve or muscle.

1Indication & principle

Requested to confirm and characterise peripheral neuropathy, to localise focal lesions (carpal tunnel, ulnar neuropathy, radiculopathy, plexopathy) and to support diagnoses such as Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), CIDP and motor neurone disease. A depolarising stimulus is applied over a nerve; motor studies record the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) from a distal muscle, sensory studies record the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP). Two properties are read off:

Amplitude reflects the number of functioning axons (or muscle fibres). Low amplitude = axon loss.
Conduction velocity & latency reflect the integrity of myelin. Slow velocity / prolonged latency / conduction block = demyelination.
2How it is performed

No specific fasting is needed; the limb should be warmed to ≥32°C because cold slows conduction and mimics demyelination. Surface electrodes stimulate the nerve at two or more points and record distally; the machine computes latency, amplitude and velocity from the distance and time between sites. Needle EMG then follows: a fine concentric needle is inserted into selected muscles and activity is assessed at rest, on minimal contraction (motor unit morphology) and on full recruitment. Multiple muscles and nerves are sampled to build a distribution that fits a root, nerve or diffuse pattern.

🧪CMAP
Motor response; amplitude = motor axon/muscle number
🧪SNAP
Sensory response; lost early in axonal neuropathy
📉F-wave
Late response; probes proximal segments & roots (early in GBS)
🔌Needle EMG
Muscle activity at rest & on contraction
3Interpretation — pattern to lesion

The decisive split is amplitude versus velocity, then EMG refines the picture.

Reduced CMAP/SNAP amplitude, velocity preserved (>70—80% normal)→AXONAL neuropathy (e.g. diabetic, alcohol, toxic)
Slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latency, conduction block, temporal dispersion→DEMYELINATING neuropathy (GBS, CIDP, CMT1)
Prolonged median distal sensory/motor latency at wrist, ulnar normal→Carpal tunnel syndrome (median neuropathy at the wrist)
EMG: fibrillations & positive sharp waves at rest→Active denervation (axon loss)
EMG: large, long-duration, polyphasic units, reduced recruitment→Chronic NEUROPATHIC / reinnervated pattern
EMG: small, short-duration, polyphasic units, early (full) recruitment→MYOPATHIC pattern (muscle disease)
Denervation confined to one myotome across muscles supplied by different nerves→Radiculopathy (root lesion)
Widespread fibrillations + fasciculations in ≥3 regions with normal sensory studies→Motor neurone disease (anterior horn cell)
4Pitfalls, timing & limitations
Timing: denervation changes (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) take ~2—3 weeks to appear on EMG, so an early study after acute injury can be falsely normal.
Temperature: a cold limb slows conduction and can mimic demyelination — always warm and record limb temperature.
Coverage: NCS reliably test only large myelinated fibres; small-fibre (thin, unmyelinated) neuropathy can give entirely normal studies.
Comfort: needle EMG is uncomfortable and operator-dependent; sampling error means a negative study does not exclude disease.
🚩 Needle EMG breaches the skin and muscle: in patients who are anticoagulated or have a coagulopathy it carries a bleeding/haematoma risk and must be planned carefully (limited muscles, avoid deep/compartmental muscles, correct or account for INR). Because denervation takes ~2—3 weeks to show, do not exclude a nerve lesion on the basis of an EMG performed too early.
🎓 One line wins the exam: AXONAL = low amplitude (velocity preserved); DEMYELINATING = slow velocity / prolonged latency / conduction block (amplitude relatively preserved). Add: normal sensory studies with widespread active denervation and fasciculations points to motor neurone disease.
Carpal tunnel confirmed (prolonged median distal latency)→nocturnal wrist splint → corticosteroid injection → surgical decompression for severe/refractory disease (thenar wasting, denervation); screen for hypothyroidism, pregnancy, acromegaly, RA, diabetes. Compression neuropathies ›
Acquired demyelinating polyneuropathy (GBS)→IVIG or plasma exchange — steroids do NOT help; monitor serial FVC for respiratory failure (ITU/ventilation) + VTE prophylaxis. Chronic, relapsing, steroid-responsive form = CIDP. Guillain–Barré ›
Denervation + fasciculations (≥3 regions), normal sensory studies→suspected motor neurone disease → urgent neurology referral; no single confirmatory test (clinical + EMG, El Escorial/Awaji). MND ›

Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) is an electrophysiological test of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ): a motor nerve is stimulated repeatedly while the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) is recorded over the muscle. It distinguishes a postsynaptic defect (myasthenia gravis, MG) from a presynaptic defect (Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome, LEMS) by the direction in which the CMAP amplitude changes across a train of stimuli.

1Indication & principle

Used to confirm an NMJ disorder in a patient with fatigable weakness (MG: ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and proximal limb weakness worsening through the day) or proximal weakness with autonomic features (LEMS). Normally each nerve impulse releases far more acetylcholine (ACh) than needed — a large “safety factor” keeps every stimulus above the threshold for muscle firing.

MG — antibodies to the postsynaptic AChR (or MuSK) reduce receptor number, so the safety factor is already low; repeated firing depletes ACh and successive responses fail → decrement.
LEMS — antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC, P/Q type) impair ACh release; at rest the resting CMAP is small, but rapid/repeated activity lets calcium accumulate, boosting release → increment / facilitation.
2How it is performed

A supramaximal stimulus is delivered to a motor nerve (commonly ulnar, accessory or facial) and a train of stimuli recorded, comparing the amplitude of the first and (typically) fourth/fifth CMAP.

Low-frequency RNS (2–3 Hz): the standard screen for MG — slow enough to deplete ACh and unmask a decrement.
High-frequency RNS (20–50 Hz) or ~10 s of maximal voluntary exercise: used for LEMS — drives calcium influx to reveal facilitation/increment.
Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. pyridostigmine) are withheld ~12 h beforehand, and the limb kept warm, as cold and drugs mask the abnormality.
3Interpretation — the numbers
Low-freq (2–3 Hz) decrement >10%→Myasthenia gravis (postsynaptic block)
Small resting CMAP + increment ≥60–100% after high-freq/exercise→LEMS (presynaptic, facilitation)
Normal RNS but clinical suspicion high→Proceed to single-fibre EMG (most sensitive test)
Increased jitter ± blocking on single-fibre EMG→Confirms NMJ transmission defect (not specific to cause)
🧪MG
Postsynaptic AChR Ab; DECREMENT on low-freq; worse with use
🧪LEMS
Presynaptic VGCC Ab; INCREMENT/facilitation; improves with use; SCLC
🔬SF-EMG
Increased jitter; most sensitive NMJ test but least specific
4Pitfalls & limitations
Low-frequency RNS is relatively insensitive, especially in purely ocular MG — a normal study does not exclude disease.
Cooling, recent pyridostigmine, or submaximal stimulation can abolish a decrement (false negative).
Single-fibre EMG is highly sensitive but not specific — increased jitter also occurs in other neuromuscular disease, so results are read with antibody and clinical data.
🚩 A confirmed LEMS pattern mandates a hunt for small-cell lung cancer (CT chest ± PET); the electrophysiology may precede the tumour by months. In MG, watch for myasthenic crisis — respiratory-muscle failure: monitor forced vital capacity (FVC), and consider ventilatory support when FVC falls below ~15 mL/kg (or ~1 L), not oxygen saturation which drops late.
🎓 Remember the direction: MG → DECREMENT on LOW-frequency stimulation; LEMS → INCREMENT / post-exercise facilitation on high-frequency stimulation. “MG tires, LEMS wires.”
Decrement confirms myasthenia gravis→send anti-AChR (then anti-MuSK if negative) and image the mediastinum (CT/MRI thymus) for thymoma (~10–15%, resectable). Neuromuscular junction disorders ›

Single-fibre electromyography (SFEMG) is a highly specialised needle-EMG technique that records action potentials from individual muscle fibres. It is the single most sensitive electrophysiological test for disorders of neuromuscular junction (NMJ) transmission, particularly myasthenia gravis (MG) — remaining positive in many patients when repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) and acetylcholine-receptor antibodies are negative, including in purely ocular disease.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

SFEMG is used when NMJ pathology is suspected but conventional tests are inconclusive — e.g. suspected ocular or seronegative MG, or a normal RNS with a convincing clinical picture. The principle rests on the concept of jitter: the small physiological variability in the time interval between the firing of two muscle fibres belonging to the same motor unit. This variability arises almost entirely from the random fluctuation in synaptic delay at each fibre's endplate.

In health, the safety factor of transmission is high, so the endplate potential reliably crosses threshold with only tiny timing variation → small jitter.
When the safety factor falls (MG), the time to reach threshold varies more from discharge to discharge → increased jitter, the earliest measurable sign of impaired transmission.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A concentric or dedicated single-fibre needle with a very small recording surface is inserted into a mildly contracting muscle. The commonest muscles are the extensor digitorum communis (limb) and frontalis or orbicularis oculi (for ocular/facial disease). Potentials from two fibres of the same motor unit are isolated during slight voluntary activation (or by axonal stimulation in unco-operative patients/children).

Consecutive interpotential intervals are recorded and the jitter expressed as the mean consecutive difference (MCD), in microseconds (µs).
Typically ~20 fibre pairs are studied to give a representative sample for the muscle.
Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. pyridostigmine) are usually withheld for several hours beforehand so they do not mask abnormal transmission.
3INTERPRETATION

Two abnormalities are sought: increased jitter and, more severely, blocking (intermittent failure of one fibre to fire at all — the endplate potential never reaches threshold). Blocking correlates with clinical weakness.

Normal jitter (MCD, EDC) < ~35 µs→Normal NMJ transmission
Increased jitter with no blocking→Early / mild NMJ transmission defect
Increased jitter WITH intermittent blocking→Clinically significant NMJ dysfunction (correlates with weakness)
Normal jitter in a symptomatic muscle→Effectively excludes MG in that muscle (very high sensitivity)
🧪Jitter (MCD)
Timing variability between two fibres of one motor unit; the core measurement
🚫Blocking
Complete intermittent failure of fibre firing; marks a severe transmission defect
🎯Fibre density
Number of single fibres per motor unit; raised in reinnervating neurogenic disease
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

SFEMG is exquisitely sensitive but its abnormality is not specific to MG. Increased jitter simply signals unstable NMJ transmission, which occurs in any process with immature or unstable endplates.

Jitter is also increased in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, motor neurone disease, peripheral neuropathies, myopathies and any active reinnervation.
It is technically demanding, operator-dependent and uncomfortable, requiring a co-operative patient able to sustain gentle contraction.
It confirms a transmission defect but does not identify its cause — antibodies and clinical assessment are still needed to reach a diagnosis.
🚩 SFEMG is sensitive but non-specific: increased jitter is not diagnostic of myasthenia gravis on its own. It must always be interpreted alongside the clinical picture, antibody status and other neurophysiology, since neurogenic and myopathic disorders also produce abnormal jitter.
🎓 High-yield: SFEMG measuring jitter is the MOST SENSITIVE test for myasthenia gravis (>95% when an appropriate muscle is studied), and can be positive when RNS is normal and AChR antibodies are negative — remember it for the seronegative or purely ocular MG patient.

The visual evoked potential (VEP) is an electrophysiological test that measures the latency of the cortical electrical response generated over the occipital cortex when the eye is stimulated with a reversing checkerboard pattern. It probes the integrity of the visual pathway from retina to occipital cortex, and is especially valuable for detecting optic nerve demyelination. In multiple sclerosis, a delayed but well-formed cortical wave (the P100) provides objective evidence of a previous or subclinical episode of optic neuritis, helping to establish dissemination of lesions in space.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

VEPs are used to find objective evidence of an optic nerve lesion, particularly a clinically silent one. Myelin allows rapid saltatory conduction; when the optic nerve is demyelinated, action potentials travel more slowly, so the cortical response arrives late. Because amplitude depends chiefly on the number of surviving axons while latency depends on conduction speed, demyelination characteristically delays the response while preserving amplitude.

Confirms a suspected optic neuropathy when fundoscopy and acuity are normal.
Detects a subclinical second lesion to support dissemination in space in suspected MS.
Documents prior optic neuritis even after visual recovery.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient sits before a screen showing a black-and-white checkerboard that reverses (pattern-reversal) once or twice per second, while occipital scalp electrodes record the response. Each eye is tested monocularly in turn, with the other eye occluded, so the two optic nerves can be compared. Responses to many reversals are averaged to extract the signal from background noise.

Refractive errors corrected and fixation maintained on a central target.
The main reproducible waveform is a large positive deflection at around 100 ms — the P100.
Both absolute latency and the interocular latency difference are recorded.
3INTERPRETATION

The key measurement is the P100 latency. A prolonged latency with a preserved, well-formed waveform points to demyelination, whereas a low-amplitude response suggests axonal loss.

P100 latency ~100 ms, symmetric→Normal optic nerve conduction
Delayed P100, amplitude preserved→Optic nerve demyelination (e.g. prior/subclinical optic neuritis)
Interocular latency difference > ~8–10 ms→Unilateral optic nerve involvement
Reduced amplitude, latency near normal→Axonal loss / ischaemic or compressive optic neuropathy
Absent response→Severe conduction block or dense axonal damage
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

The test only assesses the visual pathway, and an abnormal result localises but does not by itself give a diagnosis. Interpretation must account for factors that slow conduction or degrade the signal independently of demyelination.

Poor fixation, drowsiness, or uncorrected refractive error can degrade or delay the response.
Media opacities (cataract), maculopathy, and glaucoma can alter latency and amplitude.
A delayed P100 persists long after clinical recovery, so it reflects prior injury rather than acute activity.
🚩 A delayed VEP supports demyelination of the optic nerve but is NOT specific to multiple sclerosis — the same pattern occurs in other optic neuropathies, compressive lesions and hereditary conditions. It contributes to, but never alone establishes, a diagnosis of MS.
🎓 Delayed P100 latency with preserved amplitude = optic nerve demyelination, providing objective evidence of previous (often subclinical) optic neuritis and a second lesion in space.
Delayed P100 supports optic-nerve demyelination→next step MRI brain + cord (McDonald criteria: dissemination in space and time). Multiple sclerosis ›
🧪Stimulus
Reversing checkerboard pattern, each eye tested separately
📈P100
Positive occipital wave at ~100 ms — the key marker
🕒Latency
Delayed = demyelination (slowed conduction)
📉Amplitude
Reduced = axonal loss rather than demyelination

The electroencephalogram (EEG) records the summed electrical activity of cortical pyramidal neurons via scalp electrodes, displayed as waveforms across frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, beta). It is the key neurophysiological investigation for characterising epilepsy, detecting encephalitic and encephalopathic patterns, and supporting the diagnosis of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). Crucially, it classifies seizures and localises dysfunction rather than acting as a simple present/absent test for epilepsy.

1Indication & principle

EEG captures synchronised post-synaptic potentials of cortical neurons. In epilepsy it detects interictal epileptiform discharges (spikes and sharp waves) between seizures, helping confirm a clinical diagnosis, distinguish generalised from focal onset, and guide antiseizure drug choice.

Used to classify epilepsy syndromes, not to prove someone did or did not have a seizure.
Diffuse slowing reflects encephalopathy or encephalitis; periodic complexes suggest specific diagnoses (HSV, CJD).
EEG is not indicated to investigate uncomplicated syncope, which is diagnosed clinically and with cardiac work-up.
2How it is performed

Scalp electrodes are placed by the international 10-20 system; a standard recording lasts about 20-30 minutes. Activation procedures increase yield of epileptiform activity:

Hyperventilation — provokes 3Hz spike-and-wave in childhood absence epilepsy.
Photic stimulation — elicits a photoparoxysmal response in idiopathic generalised epilepsies.
Sleep / sleep-deprived EEG — raises sensitivity for interictal discharges.

For diagnostic uncertainty or status, prolonged / video-EEG telemetry and continuous EEG (cEEG) monitoring capture events and detect non-convulsive status epilepticus.

3Interpretation — pattern to diagnosis
Generalised 3Hz spike-and-wave→Childhood absence epilepsy
Hypsarrhythmia (chaotic high-amplitude, disorganised)→West syndrome (infantile spasms)
Focal spikes / sharp waves→Focal epilepsy (localises seizure focus)
Periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) over temporal lobe→Herpes simplex (HSV) encephalitis
Periodic sharp-wave complexes (~1Hz)→Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)
Generalised triphasic waves→Metabolic encephalopathy (e.g. hepatic)
Continuous rhythmic ictal discharge without recovery→(Non-convulsive) status epilepticus
🧪3Hz spike-wave
Absence epilepsy; provoked by hyperventilation
🌀Hypsarrhythmia
West syndrome in infants
🧠Temporal PLEDs
HSV encephalitis
⏱️Periodic sharp waves
Sporadic CJD
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
A single interictal EEG has limited sensitivity — many people with epilepsy have a normal routine recording.
Minor non-specific abnormalities occur in healthy people, so over-reading risks false labelling and inappropriate treatment.
EEG cannot diagnose syncope and should not replace ECG/cardiac assessment for transient loss of consciousness.
🚩 A normal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy — routine interictal sensitivity is only around 30-50%. Never use a single normal EEG to rule out (or a non-specific EEG to over-diagnose) epilepsy in isolation; the diagnosis remains clinical, supported by EEG.
🎓 High-yield triad: 3Hz spike-wave = childhood absence; PLEDs / temporal periodic discharges = HSV encephalitis; periodic sharp-wave complexes = CJD. Triphasic waves point to metabolic encephalopathy, and EEG has no role in diagnosing syncope.
NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__CSF Analysis:
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is the decisive bedside-to-lab investigation in suspected meningitis and other neuro-inflammatory disease. A lumbar puncture samples fluid for cell count and differential, protein, and glucose (always paired with a simultaneous serum glucose). The pattern of these three values – not any single number – separates bacterial, viral and TB/fungal causes and drives immediate treatment.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
CSF examination is indicated whenever meningitis or encephalitis is suspected, and for investigating subarachnoid haemorrhage, raised intracranial pressure states and certain inflammatory neuropathies. The biochemical logic: pyogenic bacteria consume glucose and provoke a neutrophil response, so CSF glucose falls and polymorphs rise; viruses drive a lymphocyte response without consuming glucose; mycobacteria and fungi cause an indolent lymphocytic reaction with heavy protein exudation and marked glucose consumption.
Normal protein: 0.15–0.45 g/L
Normal glucose: ~2/3 (60–70%) of serum glucose
Normal cell count: <5 cells/mm³, no neutrophils
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Under aseptic technique the patient is positioned in the left lateral decubitus or sitting position and a needle is inserted at the L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace (below the conus medullaris). Opening pressure is measured with a manometer (normal ~6–20 cmH₂O, up to ~25 borderline). Fluid is collected in sequential numbered bottles for cell count and microscopy/culture, protein and glucose, plus additional samples for PCR (viral, meningococcal, pneumococcal), Ziehl-Neelsen/TB culture and cytology as indicated.
Essential: take a paired serum glucose at the same time – CSF glucose is meaningless without it.
Send bottles promptly; cells lyse and glucose is consumed on standing.
3INTERPRETATION – THE PATTERNS
Read the triad together against the paired serum glucose.
Turbid CSF, neutrophils ↑↑, protein >1 g/L, glucose <50% serum→BACTERIAL (pyogenic) meningitis
Clear CSF, lymphocytes, protein mildly ↑ (<1 g/L), glucose normal→VIRAL meningitis
Fibrin web/clear CSF, lymphocytes, protein very high (>1–5 g/L), glucose very low→TB or fungal (e.g. Cryptococcal) meningitis
CSF glucose ratio <0.5 (<50% of serum)→Bacterial or TB/fungal – never simple viral
🧫Bacterial
Neutrophils, protein ↑↑, glucose ↓↓, turbid
🦠Viral
Lymphocytes, protein mild ↑, glucose normal, clear
🧪TB / Fungal
Lymphocytes, protein very ↑, glucose very ↓, fibrin web
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Several traps distort interpretation:
Early bacterial or partially-treated meningitis may show lymphocyte predominance, mimicking viral.
A traumatic (bloody) tap adds blood-derived cells and protein – correct roughly 1 WCC per 500–1000 RBC and ~0.01 g/L protein per 1000 RBC/mm³.
Hyperglycaemia raises CSF glucose – always use the ratio, not the absolute value.
LP is contraindicated if there are signs of raised ICP with focal deficit or coma (risk of coning) – image first.
🚩 In suspected bacterial meningitis, give empirical IV antibiotics (and steroids per NICE) IMMEDIATELY – do NOT delay treatment to obtain the LP or await CSF results. If LP is deferred for CT or the patient is too unstable, treat first and tap later; cultures may still yield an organism for several hours after the first dose.
🎓 Lock the triad: Bacterial = neutrophils + LOW glucose; Viral = lymphocytes + NORMAL glucose; TB = lymphocytes + VERY LOW glucose + VERY HIGH protein. Glucose is the discriminator between viral (normal) and TB (low) when both show lymphocytes.
Lymphocytic CSF + fever, confusion or seizures→suspect HSV encephalitis → send CSF HSV PCR and start empirical IV aciclovir immediately — do not await the result. Meningitis / encephalitis ›
Bacterial CSF pattern — empirical treatment→IV ceftriaxone (add amoxicillin if >60, immunocompromised or pregnant — Listeria cover) + IV dexamethasone; take blood cultures and meningococcal PCR. Never delay antibiotics for the LP. Meningococcal disease ›
Confirmed/suspected bacterial or meningococcal meningitis→is notifiable — inform public health urgently and arrange ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for close contacts. Notifiable diseases ›

CSF xanthochromia is the yellow discoloration of the cerebrospinal-fluid supernatant caused by bilirubin, the breakdown product of red-cell haemoglobin. It is the confirmatory bedside/laboratory test for subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) when a CT head is negative but the clinical suspicion of a “thunderclap” headache remains. Its whole value rests on correct timing and on distinguishing a genuine bleed from a traumatic lumbar puncture (LP).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used in the patient with a sudden severe headache suggestive of SAH whose CT head is non-diagnostic. After red cells enter the CSF they are lysed by enzymes in the subarachnoid space; the released oxyhaemoglobin is converted in vivo to bilirubin by macrophage haem-oxygenase. Bilirubin production is an enzymatic, time-dependent process that cannot occur in a test tube, which is exactly why it discriminates true bleeding from blood introduced at the needle.

Oxyhaemoglobin → appears early, can form in vitro from lysed cells.
Bilirubin → forms only in vivo, needs time and living cells, the specific marker of SAH.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The LP should be delayed until at least 12 hours after headache onset, allowing enough time for haemoglobin to be metabolised to bilirubin. CSF is collected in sequential bottles; a raised opening pressure is noted. The final bottle is centrifuged promptly and the supernatant examined — spectrophotometry across the visible range (450–550 nm) is the UK standard, measuring the net bilirubin absorbance, and is far more reliable than holding the tube against a white card by eye. Samples must be protected from light and processed quickly, as bilirubin degrades.

LP timing→≥12 h after headache onset (up to ~2 weeks still useful)
Preferred method→Spectrophotometry, not visual inspection
3INTERPRETATION

Bilirubin in the supernatant confirms SAH. The key exam skill is separating a true bleed from a traumatic tap, where blood is introduced by the needle and has had no time to metabolise.

Bilirubin present in supernatant→Confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage
RBC count falls between bottle 1 and bottle 4, no xanthochromia→Traumatic tap
Xanthochromia present, RBC count constant across bottles→True SAH
🧪Bilirubin
In-vivo breakdown product, specific for SAH
🩸Oxyhaemoglobin
Early pigment, can arise in vitro, less specific
💉Traumatic tap
RBCs clear bottle-to-bottle, no bilirubin
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS

An LP performed too early may be falsely negative. Deep jaundice, a very high CSF protein, or dietary carotenaemia can raise supernatant absorbance and mimic xanthochromia, which is why spectrophotometry reports net bilirubin against oxyhaemoglobin. Delay beyond about two weeks risks a false negative as pigment clears.

🚩 An LP done before 12 hours may miss xanthochromia because bilirubin has not yet formed — timing is essential and a negative early tap does not exclude SAH. A normal non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset (read by an experienced reporter) largely excludes SAH; beyond 6 hours an LP is required.
🎓 Xanthochromia is the discriminator: it is present in true SAH but absent in a traumatic tap, and in a traumatic tap the red-cell count falls progressively from the first to the last bottle.
Xanthochromia positive — confirms SAH→→ CT angiography to localise the aneurysm + urgent neurosurgery/interventional referral; start nimodipine to reduce vasospasm. Intracranial haemorrhages ›

CSF oligoclonal bands (OCBs) are discrete bands of immunoglobulin (IgG) detected by isoelectric focusing (IEF) of cerebrospinal fluid, run side-by-side with a paired serum sample. Bands present in CSF but absent from serum prove that IgG is being synthesised within the central nervous system (intrathecal synthesis) rather than leaking from blood. This pattern is a supportive laboratory marker of the inflammatory, immune-mediated demyelination seen in multiple sclerosis (MS).

1Indication & principle

Requested when demyelinating disease, especially MS, is suspected on clinical/MRI grounds, or when a first demyelinating event needs supporting evidence. In MS a compartmentalised population of B-cells and plasma cells produces IgG behind the blood–brain barrier. IEF separates these immunoglobulins by their isoelectric point, resolving the restricted (clonal) antibody population into visible discrete bands.

Paired CSF and serum must always be run together on the same gel – interpretation depends entirely on the comparison.
The finding of intrathecal IgG reflects chronic CNS inflammation, not a single pathogen.
2How it is performed

CSF is obtained by lumbar puncture and a simultaneous blood sample is taken for serum. Both are subjected to isoelectric focusing followed by IgG-specific immunofixation/immunoblotting – the current gold-standard method, more sensitive than older agarose electrophoresis. Laboratories also calculate the IgG index from paired CSF and serum IgG and albumin to quantify intrathecal synthesis and confirm barrier integrity.

🧪CSF IgG
Numerator of the index; raised with intrathecal production
🩸Serum IgG
Comparator to exclude systemic/leaked immunoglobulin
🧫Albumin (CSF & serum)
Q-albumin assesses blood–brain barrier integrity
📊IgG index
(CSF IgG/serum IgG) ÷ (CSF albumin/serum albumin)
3Interpretation

The pattern of bands in CSF relative to serum defines the result. Two or more bands unique to CSF is the abnormal, MS-supportive finding.

≥2 bands in CSF, none in serum→Intrathecal IgG synthesis – supports MS (positive OCBs)
Identical (mirror) bands in CSF & serum→Systemic immune activation, NOT intrathecal – negative for MS
No bands in either→Negative – does not support MS
IgG index > 0.7→Quantitatively raised intrathecal IgG production
CSF-specific OCBs in a clinically isolated syndrome→McDonald criteria – can substitute for dissemination in time
4Pitfalls & limitations

OCBs indicate CNS inflammation, not MS specifically. Positive CSF-restricted bands also occur in CNS infections (e.g. neurosyphilis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, HIV, chronic viral encephalitis), neurosarcoidosis, and CNS involvement of systemic autoimmune disease such as SLE. A mirror pattern (bands in both compartments) reflects a systemic process and must not be over-read as intrathecal. Absence of OCBs does not fully exclude MS, but MS with negative bands is uncommon and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

🚩 Only bands present in CSF and absent from paired serum count – without the serum comparison a positive result is uninterpretable. OCBs are not specific to MS: always exclude CNS infection and other inflammatory/autoimmune causes before attributing them to demyelination.
🎓 High-yield: CSF-only (unmatched) oligoclonal bands support a diagnosis of MS and, under the McDonald criteria, can substitute for demonstrating dissemination in time in a patient with a clinically isolated syndrome.

Albuminocytological dissociation is the classic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS): a raised CSF protein with a normal white cell count. The “dissociation” is between the high albumin/protein and the normal cellularity. It reflects inflammation of the spinal nerve roots and, together with nerve conduction studies and the clinical picture of ascending weakness with areflexia, supports the diagnosis of an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Lumbar puncture is performed in a patient with suspected GBS — progressive, roughly symmetrical ascending weakness with hyporeflexia or areflexia, often following a preceding infection (e.g. Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV). Inflammation and demyelination at the level of the nerve roots increases the permeability of the blood-nerve barrier, allowing protein (mainly albumin) to leak into the CSF while there is little or no cellular infiltrate.

Purpose: support the clinical diagnosis and, importantly, exclude mimics (infection, malignant infiltration).
CSF is only one leg of the diagnosis — the others are the clinical syndrome and nerve conduction studies showing a demyelinating pattern.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A standard lumbar puncture is done at the L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace with the patient positioned laterally or sitting. CSF is sent for protein, glucose (with a paired serum glucose), cell count and differential, microscopy, culture and, where indicated, virology/cytology.

Timing matters: the CSF may be normal in the first week of symptoms, with protein typically rising after ~1–2 weeks.
A normal early tap does not exclude GBS — if clinical suspicion is high, treat and consider repeating the LP.
3INTERPRETATION

The hallmark is a raised protein with a normal cell count. Interpret the numbers together:

Protein > 0.45 g/L with WCC ≤ 5 cells/mm³→Albuminocytological dissociation — supports GBS
Normal protein in first ~7 days→Does not exclude GBS; repeat after 1–2 weeks
WCC > 10 cells/mm³ (pleocytosis)→Argues against GBS — seek infection, malignancy or HIV
Normal glucose, no organisms on Gram stain→Consistent with non-infective inflammatory process
🧪CSF protein
Raised (> 0.45 g/L); may be markedly high after 1–2 weeks
🔬CSF cells
Normal (≤ 5 cells/mm³) — the “dissociation”
⚡Nerve conduction
Demyelinating: slowed conduction, conduction block, prolonged F-waves
🩺Clinical
Ascending weakness with areflexia post-infection
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Sensitivity is time-dependent — up to half of patients have normal protein in the first few days.
A raised cell count is the key red herring: it points away from GBS toward an alternative diagnosis.
Albuminocytological dissociation is not unique to GBS — it can occur in CIDP and some spinal/root pathologies, so it is supportive, not pathognomonic.
🚩 A raised CSF cell count (pleocytosis) argues AGAINST GBS — consider infection, malignant meningitis or HIV seroconversion (test for HIV). GBS itself carries a risk of neuromuscular respiratory failure and autonomic instability: monitor Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) serially, and treat with IVIG or plasma exchange — not corticosteroids.
🎓 High CSF protein + normal cell count = albuminocytological dissociation = Guillain-Barré syndrome. If the cells are up, think again.

CSF opening pressure is the pressure of cerebrospinal fluid measured with a manometer at the moment of lumbar puncture, while the patient lies still in the lateral decubitus position. It is a single, powerful bedside number that separates the raised-pressure syndromes (above all idiopathic intracranial hypertension) from low-pressure leaks and from the deceptively normal pressure of NPH — and in some conditions the tap that measures it is also the treatment.

1Indication & principle
CSF is produced by the choroid plexus (~500 mL/day) and absorbed at the arachnoid granulations; a steady state sets a normal pressure. Measuring opening pressure at LP quantifies that balance and is central to diagnosing raised-ICP states with normal parenchyma. Key uses:
Suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — headache, papilloedema, visual loss in a typically obese young woman.
Suspected normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — gait apraxia, cognitive decline and urinary incontinence.
Suspected spontaneous intracranial hypotension — orthostatic headache from a CSF leak.
Valid readings require the legs and neck to be relaxed and the manometer zeroed at the level of the needle, because a truly reliable pressure can only be read in the lateral decubitus position (a sitting patient gives a falsely high hydrostatic column).
2How it is performed
Position: left lateral decubitus, back at the couch edge, hips and knees flexed but then partially relaxed with the neck neutral for the reading.
Access: aseptic technique, needle at the L3/L4 or L4/L5 interspace (below the conus at ~L1/L2).
Measure: once free flow is obtained, attach the three-way tap and manometer and let the CSF column rise until it plateaus and oscillates gently with respiration — that plateau is the opening pressure in cmH₂O.
Then sample: collect CSF for cell count, protein, glucose (with paired serum glucose) and microbiology after the pressure is recorded.
In IIH, therapeutic drainage of CSF to a normal closing pressure can be performed at the same sitting. In suspected NPH, a large-volume “tap test” removes ~30–50 mL and gait is reassessed before and after.
3Interpretation & cut-offs
6–20 cmH₂O (up to ~25)→Normal adult opening pressure
>25 cmH₂O with normal imaging & normal CSF constituents→Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
<6 cmH₂O (often unrecordably low)→Intracranial hypotension / CSF leak
Normal pressure + triad + gait improves after large-volume tap→Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — predicts shunt response
Raised pressure + abnormal CSF/imaging→Secondary cause (mass, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis) — not IIH
🔺IIH
>25 cmH₂O, normal scan & CSF; obese young women; papilloedema, visual loss
🔻Hypotension
<6 cmH₂O; orthostatic headache; CSF leak
🧠NPH
Normal pressure; dementia, gait apraxia, incontinence; tap improves gait
🧪Secondary
Raised pressure with abnormal CSF/imaging — seek a cause
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
A sitting position, straining, breath-holding, a tense/flexed patient or obesity all falsely raise the reading — relax the patient and read in lateral decubitus.
Pressure fluctuates with respiration and the cardiac cycle; take the mean plateau, not a transient peak.
A traumatic or dry tap, or measuring before free CSF flow, gives an unreliable value.
In NPH a single normal opening pressure does not exclude the diagnosis — the functional response to CSF removal is what matters.
🚩 Never perform LP to measure opening pressure when raised ICP is due to a suspected mass lesion or there are focal signs / reduced consciousness — removing CSF below can precipitate fatal tonsillar herniation (coning). Image the brain first. In confirmed IIH the priority is to protect vision: monitor visual fields and treat urgently, as untreated raised pressure can cause permanent blindness.
🎓 In the exam, an opening pressure >25 cmH₂O with a normal CT/MRI and normal CSF constituents in an obese young woman with headache and papilloedema is IIH — and draining CSF to a normal closing pressure at that same LP is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
Before any LP — other contraindications→coagulopathy, platelets <50, therapeutic anticoagulation (check clotting/platelets and stop/reverse first) and local skin sepsis at the puncture site — as well as raised ICP / a mass lesion (image first).
NEUROPHYSIOLOGY & CSF__CSF — Specialised:
CSF prion diagnostics are the bedside-to-lab tests used to confirm Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in a patient with a rapidly progressive dementia. Two CSF assays dominate: the 14-3-3 protein, a non-specific marker of fast neuronal destruction, and RT-QuIC (real-time quaking-induced conversion), a highly specific assay that directly detects misfolded prion protein. Together with clinical features (myoclonus, cerebellar/visual signs), EEG and MRI, they underpin the modern diagnostic criteria for sporadic CJD.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Requested when a patient presents with a rapidly progressive dementia (cognitive decline over weeks to months) plus features suggesting prion disease. The underlying pathology is conversion of normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into a misfolded, protease-resistant isoform (PrPSc) that aggregates and drives spongiform neurodegeneration.

14-3-3 is an abundant intraneuronal protein released into CSF when neurons are rapidly destroyed — it is a marker of how fast neurons are dying, not of prions specifically.
RT-QuIC exploits the seeding property of PrPSc: a trace of misfolded protein in the CSF templates recombinant PrP substrate to misfold and aggregate, generating an amplifiable signal.
🧠Rapidly progressive dementia
Cognitive decline over weeks–months
⚡Myoclonus
Often startle-induced jerks
📈EEG periodic sharp waves
~1 Hz periodic complexes (sporadic CJD)
🧲MRI DWI change
Cortical ribboning & basal ganglia restriction
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Both assays are run on cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture. Standard opening pressure, cell count, protein and glucose are checked (usually near-normal in CJD, which helps exclude infective/inflammatory mimics). A dedicated CSF aliquot is sent to a national prion reference laboratory (in the UK, the National CJD Research & Surveillance Unit).

Sample handling must avoid blood contamination, which can cause false-positive 14-3-3.
RT-QuIC incubates patient CSF with recombinant prion substrate under cyclical shaking (“quaking”); aggregation is read in real time via a fluorescent dye (thioflavin T) over ~40–90 hours.
Results are interpreted alongside EEG and MRI DWI — no single test stands alone.
3INTERPRETATION
RT-QuIC positive→Highly specific (>98%) for CJD — a diagnostic criterion for probable sporadic CJD
14-3-3 positive/raised→Supports rapid neuronal loss but NOT specific — also seen in stroke, encephalitis, hypoxia, seizures
EEG periodic sharp-wave complexes (~1 Hz)→Supportive of sporadic CJD (often absent in variant CJD)
MRI DWI cortical “ribboning” + caudate/putamen hyperintensity→Strongly supportive; pulvinar sign favours variant CJD
RT-QuIC negative but high clinical suspicion→Does not exclude CJD — repeat CSF and continue MRI/EEG surveillance
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
14-3-3 has poor specificity — a positive result in any acute neuronal-destructive process (recent stroke, viral encephalitis, status epilepticus) can mislead.
Sensitivity of RT-QuIC is good but imperfect; an early or atypical case may test negative, so a negative result never rules out disease.
Diagnosis is clinicopathological — definitive confirmation is neuropathology (brain biopsy or post-mortem), rarely needed if CSF/MRI criteria are met.
🚩 CJD is TRANSMISSIBLE and prions RESIST standard decontamination — they survive routine autoclaving, formalin and standard sterilisation. Use single-use instruments where possible for LP and any neurosurgical procedure, quarantine/incinerate reusable instruments per national prion guidance, and label CSF samples as high-risk. There is NO curative treatment; care is supportive and the disease is invariably fatal (typically within months of onset in sporadic CJD).
🎓 Exam gold: 14-3-3 is sensitive but non-specific; RT-QuIC is highly specific for CJD. If a stem describes rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and a positive CSF RT-QuIC, the answer is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

CSF herpes simplex virus (HSV) PCR is a nucleic-acid amplification test that detects HSV DNA in cerebrospinal fluid. It is the definitive investigation for herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) — the commonest sporadic fatal viral encephalitis in the UK — and has largely replaced brain biopsy. HSE is a medical emergency: the role of the PCR is to confirm a diagnosis that must already be treated empirically.

1Indication & principle

Suspect HSE in any patient with the triad of fever, altered consciousness/behavioural change and seizures, often with focal (temporal-lobe) features such as dysphasia, memory disturbance or personality change. HSV (usually HSV-1) has a predilection for the temporal and inferior frontal lobes. PCR amplifies viral DNA directly from CSF, allowing rapid, biopsy-free diagnosis with very high accuracy.

Sensitivity ≈ 96%, specificity ≈ 99% once established.
Supportive tests: MRI showing temporal-lobe hyperintensity/oedema; EEG showing lateralised periodic temporal discharges (PLEDs).
2How it is performed

Perform a lumbar puncture once safe (exclude raised ICP / mass effect — CT first if reduced GCS, focal deficit or papilloedema, but do NOT let imaging delay treatment). Send CSF for real-time HSV-1/2 DNA PCR alongside cell count, protein, glucose (with paired serum glucose), and opening pressure. A small sterile CSF aliquot is required; results typically return within hours to a day.

🧪HSV PCR
Detects viral DNA — the confirmatory test
🔬CSF cells
Lymphocytosis — viral pattern
🩸CSF protein
Mildly-moderately raised
🍬CSF glucose
Normal — helps exclude bacterial
3Interpretation
HSV PCR POSITIVE→Confirms HSV encephalitis — complete full IV aciclovir course
CSF lymphocytes typically 10–500 ×10⁶/L→Lymphocytic (viral) picture; RBCs may be raised (haemorrhagic necrosis)
CSF protein > 0.45 g/L, glucose normal (≥ 60% of serum)→Supports viral encephalitis, argues against bacterial meningitis
HSV PCR NEGATIVE within first 24–72 h of symptoms→Does NOT exclude HSE — continue aciclovir and REPEAT PCR at 72 h–7 days
4Pitfalls & limitations
Early false negatives: viral DNA may be undetectable in the first 24–72 h — a normal-appearing CSF or negative PCR very early is unreliable.
False negatives also from prior aciclovir clearing DNA, or haem/heparin PCR inhibitors — do not delay LP for sampling reasons.
A completely normal CSF occurs in a minority early; clinical, MRI and EEG evidence still mandate treatment.
🚩 Start IV aciclovir IMMEDIATELY on clinical suspicion — do NOT wait for the PCR result. Each hour of delay increases mortality and long-term neurological disability. A negative early PCR does not exclude HSE: continue treatment and repeat the PCR. Untreated HSE mortality is around 70%.
🎓 Golden rule: treat first, confirm second. Empirical IV aciclovir goes in on suspicion; the CSF HSV PCR is the confirmatory test, not the trigger to treat. Temporal-lobe changes on MRI + lymphocytic CSF in an encephalopathic febrile patient = HSE until proven otherwise.

CSF orexin-A (also called hypocretin-1) is a hypothalamic neuropeptide that promotes wakefulness and stabilises the boundary between sleep and wake states. Measuring its concentration in cerebrospinal fluid is a highly specific diagnostic test for narcolepsy type 1 (narcolepsy with cataplexy), in which autoimmune destruction of orexin-producing neurons leaves CSF levels low or undetectable.

1Indication & principle

Orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus project widely to arousal centres and are essential for maintaining stable wakefulness and suppressing inappropriate REM intrusion. In narcolepsy type 1 an autoimmune process (strongly linked to HLA-DQB1*06:02) destroys these neurons, so orexin falls dramatically in the CSF.

Used when narcolepsy is suspected but the sleep study is equivocal or cannot be reliably interpreted.
Cataplexy — sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (classically laughter) — is the clinical hallmark that points to type 1.
Associated REM-dissociation phenomena: sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.
2How it is performed

CSF is obtained by lumbar puncture and orexin-A is quantified by radioimmunoassay, ideally against a standardised reference so values are comparable between laboratories.

A standard aseptic lumbar puncture is performed; only a small CSF aliquot is needed.
Samples should be handled and stored appropriately (frozen) as orexin is labile, and assayed against the reference standard.
The result is interpreted alongside clinical features and, where done, the multiple sleep latency test (MSLT).
3Interpretation
CSF orexin-A ≤ 110 pg/mL (or < one-third of normal mean)→Diagnostic of narcolepsy type 1 (with cataplexy)
CSF orexin-A > 200 pg/mL→Normal — narcolepsy type 1 effectively excluded
MSLT: mean sleep latency ≤ 8 min + ≥ 2 sleep-onset REM periods→Supports narcolepsy; complements the orexin result
Normal/intermediate orexin with typical MSLT but no cataplexy→Favours narcolepsy type 2 (orexin usually preserved)
4Pitfalls & limitations
It is an invasive test requiring lumbar puncture, so it is not first-line; the MSLT (with prior overnight polysomnography) remains the usual initial investigation.
Assay values vary between laboratories — use of the standardised reference and the ≤ 110 pg/mL cut-off is essential.
Low orexin is not fully specific in all contexts: rare acute brain injury or severe CNS pathology can transiently lower levels, so results are read in clinical context.
🧪CSF orexin-A
Low/undetectable in narcolepsy type 1
🧬HLA-DQB1*06:02
Strong genetic association
😴MSLT
Short latency + sleep-onset REM
💥Cataplexy
Emotion-triggered muscle-tone loss
🚩 A low CSF orexin-A (≤ 110 pg/mL) is highly specific for narcolepsy type 1 and effectively confirms the diagnosis, but the test is reserved for equivocal MSLT cases or where the sleep study is unreliable — it should not be used as an indiscriminate screen.
🎓 Remember the equation: low CSF orexin/hypocretin-1 = narcolepsy type 1 = narcolepsy WITH cataplexy, HLA-DQB1*06:02 positive. Narcolepsy type 2 (without cataplexy) has normal orexin.
